Holonomy and parallel transport in the differential geometry of the space of loops and the groupoid of generalized gauge transformationsThanks: C. A. Rossi acknowledges partial support of Aly Kaufman Fellowship

Carlo A. Rossi Address: Dept. of Mathematics — Technion — 32000 Haifa — Israel Email address: crossi@techunix.technion.ac.il
Abstract.

The motivation for this paper stems [4] from the need to construct explicit isomorphisms of (possibly nontrivial) principal GG-bundles on the space of loops or, more generally, of paths in some manifold MM, over which I consider a fixed principal bundle PP; the aforementioned bundles are then pull-backs of PP w.r.t. evaluation maps at different points.

The explicit construction of these isomorphisms between pulled-back bundles relies on the notion of parallel transport. I introduce and discuss extensively at this point the notion of generalized gauge transformation between (a priori) distinct principal GG-bundles over the same base MM; one can see immediately that the parallel transport can be viewed as a generalized gauge transformation for two special kind of bundles on the space of loops or paths; at this point, it is possible to generalize the previous arguments for more general pulled-back bundles.

Finally, I discuss how flatness of the reference connection, w.r.t. which I consider holonomy and parallel transport, is related to horizontality of the associated generalized gauge transformation.

1. Introduction

In the last section of [4], where the Topological Quantum Field theoretical background behind the higher-order cohomology groups of the space of knots in ℝm{\mathbb{R}}^{m}, for m≥3m\geq 3, of Cattaneo–Cotta-Ramusino–Longoni [2] was explicitly constructed, some hints were mentioned towards possible generalizations of the computations in [4], dealing with iterated Chen-type integrals, to a nontrivial principal GG-bundle PP; in fact, the main object throughout the paper was the so-called generalized holonomy, viewed as an iterated integral, on some fixed principal GG-bundle PP, which we assumed to be trivial in order to simplify the computations.

In the last section, we addressed informally the problem of defining iterated integrals, as our expression for the parallel transport, for a nontrivial bundle PP. The same problem arises also in Section 2 of [3]: the authors discuss the notion of iterated Chen integrals in relationship with so-called “special connections” on the space of horizontal paths in a (not necessarily trivial) principal bundle over a 44-manifold MM, namely they need iterated Chen integrals of forms of the adjoint type on MM in order to compute the curvature of special connections. An explicit formula is displayed there for the Chen bracket; still, as the authors themselves pointed out, it is without details, to which they planned to dedicate some further paper. One of the main subtleties of the task in [3] and [4] lies therein, that we need to identify pulled-back bundles of PP on the space of loops (or, more generally, of paths) in a general manifold MM w.r.t. evaluation maps at different points. We sketched without details therein some arguments leading to the answer; in particular, we pointed out the importance in this task of the holonomy and, more generally, of the parallel transport. In fact, the parallel transport, which depends explicitly by its very construction on a connection AA on PP, defines an isomorphism between two particular type of pulled-back bundles on the space of loops or paths in MM.

In the present paper, I explain all details of this construction, performing the complete computations we hinted at in the last section of [4]. The paper is organised as follows: in Section 2, I recall the main notions, namely connections on principal GG-bundles over the manifold MM, and I discuss the two equivalent ways of defining a connection, since I will make use of them both in the subsequent computations.

In Section 3, I recall the notions of holonomy w.r.t. a chosen connection AA of a loop γ\gamma in MM and parallel transport w.r.t. AA of a path γ\gamma; I then state and prove two technical lemmata containing information about some sort of equivariance displayed by holonomy and parallel transport w.r.t. the actions of the structure group GG of PP and the gauge group 𝒢P\mathcal{G}_{P}of PP. The contents of the first two sections are standard facts in gauge theory; I will nonetheless review them in some detail to fix conventions and notations.

In Section 4, I discuss the notion of isomorphisms of GG-principal bundles (a priori distinct) over MM.It is well known that fibre-preserving, GG-equivariant automorphisms of a fixed GG-principal bundles are in one-to-one correspondence to maps from PP to GG, equivariant w.r.t. conjugation on GG; similarly, fibre-preserving, GG-equivariant (iso)morphisms between (a priori distinct) principal GG-bundles over the same base space MM are in one-to-one correspondence to what I call generalized gauge transformations. These are maps from the fibred product of the aforementioned bundles (a concept somehow mimicking the notion of Whitney sum of vector bundles) with values in GG, equivariant w.r.t. an action of the product group G×GG\times G on GG, which, when restricted to the diagonal subgroup GG, restricts to the conjugation on GG. The key element of the above correspondence lies in the canonical map from the fibred product of a bundle PP with itself associated to the identity map of PP; I also discuss its properties. I then proceed with the discussion of the structure of the set of generalized gauge transformations; it turns out to be (obviously) a groupoid over the category of principal GG-bundles over MM; this notion generalizes that of gauge group, and I therefore speak of the groupoid of generalized gauge transformations of MM and GG.

In Section 5, I partly review, partly explain some general constructions for groupoids; in particular, I recall the concept of actions of groupoids on sets and construct what I call the generalized conjugation for groupoids, which is an action of the product of a groupoid with itself on the groupoid itself, which mimics somehow the conjugation of a group on itself, a notion which no longer makes sense for a groupoid. I also discuss the notion of equivariant morphisms from (left or right) groupoid actions to other (left or right) groupoid actions.

In Section 6, I interpret holonomy and parallel transport as generalized gauge transformations for a particular type of pulled-back bundles over the space of loops or paths in MM of a fixed principal bundle PP over MM w.r.t. evaluation maps. Thus, there is a map associating to a connection on PP a generalized gauge transformation; interpreting the gauge group of PP as a groupoid, hence the space of connections on PP as a 𝒢P\mathcal{G}_{P}-space, the technical lemmata of Section 3 may be interpreted in the sense that there is an equivariant map of groupoid actions from the space of connections to the groupoid of generalized gauge transformations.

In Section 7, I discuss the important consequences of the restriction of the map discussed in Section 6 between the space of connections and the groupoid of generalized gauge transformations to the space of flat connections. Namely, the flatness (which has a non-abelian cohomological interpretation) implies in a highly nontrivial way the horizontality of a the corresponding generalized gauge transformation; the key step for this achieving this result lies in the well-known fact that flat connections induce representations of the homotopy group of MM.

Acknowledgment.

I thank A. S. Cattaneo and G. Felder for many inspiring suggestions, mainly on the subject of groupoids and for constant support; I also acknowledge the pleasant atmosphere at the Department of Mathematics of the Technion, where this work was accomplished.

2. Background definitions

In this section, I introduce the main notions and notations I use throughout the paper; among them, I want to discuss in detail the notion of connection on principal bundles. Let me notice that I work on a general principal bundle P​↦𝜋​MP\overset{\pi}{\mapsto}M over a real manifold MM (if not otherwise stated, MM is assumed to be connected and paracompact); I do not assume any particular property on the structure group GG. By 𝔤\mathfrak{g} I denote the corresponding Lie algebra.

Definition 2.1.

A connection 11-form on the principal bundle PP is a 11-form AA on PP with values in 𝔤\mathfrak{g}, satisfying the two following requirements:

  • i)

    (Equivariance)

    (2.1) Rg∗​A=Ad⁡(g−1)​A,\raction_{g}^{*}\!A=\Ad\!(g^{-1})A,

    where by Rg\raction_{g} I have denoted the (free) right action of GG on PP.

  • ii)

    (Verticality) For any ξ∈𝔤\xi\in\mathfrak{g},

    (2.2) Ap​(Te⁡Lp⁡(ξ))=ξ,∀p∈P;A_{p}\!\left(\tange\!_{e}{\laction_{p}}\!(\xi)\right)=\xi,\quad\forall p\in P;

    here, I have denoted by Rp\raction_{p} the fibre injection G→PG\to P given by g↦p​gg\mapsto pg.

For our purposes, it is better to introduce a slightly different characterisation of connections; later, I will discuss the relationship between them.

First of all, a tangent vector XX to PP at the point pp is said to be vertical, if it satisfies the equation

Tp⁡π⁡(X)=0.\tange\!_{p}{\pi}(X)=0.

The vertical space Vp⁡P\verti_{p}\!P, consisting of all vertical tangent vectors at pp, for any p∈Pp\in P, is isomorphic to the Lie-algebra 𝔤\mathfrak{g} via

ξ↦Te⁡Lp⁡(ξ),ξ∈𝔤.\xi\mapsto\tange\!_{e}{\laction_{p}}(\xi),\quad\xi\in\mathfrak{g}.

It turns out that the vertical spaces Vp⁡P\verti_{p}\!P can be glued together to give a smooth vector bundle, the so-called vertical bundle V⁡P\verti\!P (whose typical fibre is isomorphic to the Lie algebra 𝔤\mathfrak{g}); it is clearly a subbundle of T⁡P\tange\!\!P.

Alas, there is in principle no canonical way to define a complement of V⁡P\verti\!P w.r.t. Whitney sum, i.e. there is no canonical bundle H⁡P\coh\!P such that V⁡P⊕H⁡P=T⁡P\verti\!P\oplus\coh\!P=\tange\!\!P. It turns out that the choice of such a complementary bundle relies on the choice of a connection 11-form AA on PP, as it is motivated by the following definition:

Definition 2.2.

Given a connection 11-form AA on PP, a tangent vector XpX_{p} to PP at pp is said to be AA-horizontal if the following equation holds:

Ap​(Xp)=0.A_{p}\!\left(X_{p}\right)=0.

(For the sake of brevity, when the connection 11-form AA is clear from the context, I simply speak of horizontal vectors.)

2.1. The bridge between connection 11-forms and horizontal bundle

I discuss, for the sake of completeness, how a connection 11-form AA on PP gives rise to a smooth assignment to any p∈Pp\in P of a subspace Hp⁡P⊂Tp⁡P\coh_{p}\!P\subset\tange\!_{p}{P}, such that the following two requirements hold:

  • i)

    Tp⁡P=Vp⁡P⊕Hp⁡P\tange\!_{p}{P}=\verti_{p}\!P\oplus\coh_{p}\!P;

  • ii)

    Hp​g⁡P=Tp⁡Rg⁡(Hp⁡P)\coh_{pg}\!P=\tange\!_{p}{\raction_{g}}\left(\coh_{p}\!P\right), for any g∈Gg\in G,

and vice versa. In fact, the two requirements listed above are also an alternative definition of connection as a way of splitting the tangent bundle of PP into the Whitney sum of the vertical bundle, which is clearly GG-invariant as a consequence of the identity

Rg∘Lp=Lp​g∘c⁡(g−1),∀p∈P,g∈G,\raction_{g}\circ\!\laction_{p}=\laction_{pg}\circ\!\conj\!\left(g^{-1}\right),\quad\forall p\in P,g\in G,

and some horizontal bundle.

Given such an assignment, it is possible to define a corresponding connection 11-form via

(2.3) Ap​(Xp):=ξXp,A_{p}\!\left(X_{p}\right)\colon=\xi_{X_{p}},

where ξXp\xi_{X_{p}} is the unique element of 𝔤\mathfrak{g} which corresponds to the vertical part of XpX_{p} w.r.t. the above splitting, i.e.

Te⁡Lp⁡(ξXp)=Xpv,\tange\!_{e}{\laction_{p}}\!\left(\xi_{X_{p}}\right)=X_{p}^{v},

where XpvX_{p}^{v} is the vertical part of XpX_{p} w.r.t. the above splitting. It follows immediately that the horizontal space at p∈Pp\in P is exactly the kernel of ApA_{p}. The very definition of vertical space and Equation (2.3) imply together that AA satisfies (2.2). The invariance given by Condition ii) above ensures that both projections into vertical and horizontal subspace are GG-invariant, which in turn leads to (2.1).

On the other hand, given a connection 11-form AA on PP, the corresponding splitting of T⁡P\tange\!\!P at some point p∈Pp\in P is given by

Xp=(Xp−XpA)+XpA,XpA:=Te⁡Lp⁡(Ap​(Xp)),p∈P.X_{p}=\left(X_{p}-X_{p}^{A}\right)+X_{p}^{A},\quad X_{p}^{A}\colon=\tange\!_{e}{\laction_{p}}\!\left(A_{p}(X_{p})\right),\quad p\in P.

In fact, by (2.2), it is easy to prove that the linear operator Te⁡Lp∘Ap\tange\!_{e}{\laction_{p}}\!\circ\!A_{p} is the projection onto the vertical subspace; its kernel is therefore the horizontal subspace corresponding to the choice of AA. Condition (2.1), in turn, alongside the identity

Lp​g∘c⁡(g−1)=Rg∘Lp,∀p∈P,g∈G,\laction_{pg}\circ\conj\!\left(g^{-1}\right)=\raction_{g}\circ\laction_{p},\quad\forall p\in P,g\in G,

ensures that the corresponding distribution is GG-equivariant (c\conj denotes the conjugation on GG). Finally, let me spend some words on the concept of gauge transformation of a principal GG-bundle PP over MM. A gauge transformation σ\sigma of PP is a (smooth) map from PP to PP, enjoying the following two properties:

π∘σ=π,σ⁡(p​g)=σ⁡(p)​g,∀p∈P,g∈G.\pi\circ\sigma=\pi,\quad\sigma(pg)=\sigma(p)g,\quad\forall p\in P,g\in G.

The first condition means that any gauge transformation respects the fibres of PP; the second one means that σ\sigma is equivariant w.r.t. the (right) GG-action on PP. Later, we will see that there is another way of defining gauge transformations of a bundle PP, but, for the moment, let me skip the problem.

Another problem I will address to later is that, in fact, any gauge transformation is an isomorphism; the proof of this fact is easy, but I prefer to postpone it to Section 4, deserving it a treatment in a more general context.

Let me notice that this last fact that means that the set of gauge transformations is a group w.r.t. the product operation given by composition; hence, it makes sense to speak of the gauge group of a principal bundle PP, which I denote by 𝒢P\mathcal{G}_{P}.

Finally, the gauge group 𝒢P\mathcal{G}_{P} operates on the space of connections on PP, which I denote by 𝒜=𝒜P\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{A}_{P}, to make manifest the dependence on the chosen bundle PP; the (right) action is given explicitly by

Aσ:=σ∗​A,A∈𝒜P,σ∈𝒢P.A^{\sigma}\colon=\sigma^{*}A,\quad A\in\mathcal{A}_{P},\sigma\in\mathcal{G}_{P}.

3. Holonomy and parallel transport

Let me consider a curve γ\gamma on MM; by the word “curve”, I mean in this context (if not otherwise stated) a piecewise smooth map from the unit interval I\mathrm{I} to MM.

Definition 3.1.

Given a connection 11-form AA on PP, a horizontal lift of γ\gamma based at p∈Pp\in P is a curve on PP, lying over γ\gamma, based at the point pp and such that all its tangent directions are (AA-)horizontal.

I quote without proof from [7], Chapter 2, Section 3, the following Theorem, which is the main ingredient of many of the subsequent constructions:

Theorem 3.2.

Given a connection 11-form AA on PP and a curve γ\gamma in MM, there is a unique horizontal lift of γ\gamma based at the point pp, which I denote by γ~A,p\widetilde{\gamma}_{A,p}.

Now, it is possible to display two important consequences of Theorem 3.2.

3.1. Holonomy: definition and main properties

I consider a loop γ\gamma, i.e. a curve in MM satisfying γ⁡(0)=γ⁡(1)\gamma(0)=\gamma(1); I choose additionally a point p∈Pp\in P lying over γ⁡(0)=γ⁡(1)\gamma(0)=\gamma(1). Given a connection AA, by Theorem 3.2, there is a unique horizontal lift γ~A,p\widetilde{\gamma}_{A,p} of γ\gamma based at pp. Since γ~A,p\widetilde{\gamma}_{A,p} is a lift of γ\gamma, γ~A,p​(1)\widetilde{\gamma}_{A,p}(1) also lies over γ⁡(0)\gamma(0), and, as GG acts transitively on each fibre of PP, it makes sense to propose the following

Definition 3.3.

The holonomy of γ\gamma w.r.t. the connection AA and base point pp over γ⁡(0)\gamma(0) is the unique element of GG, usually denoted by H⁡(A,γ,p)\partr\!\left(A;\gamma;p\right), satisfying

(3.1) γ~A,p​(1)=p​H⁡(A,γ,p),\widetilde{\gamma}_{A,p}(1)=p\!\partr\!\left(A;\gamma;p\right),

where γ~A,p\widetilde{\gamma}_{A,p} is the unique horizontal lift based at p∈Pp\in P over γ⁡(0)\gamma(0), of the loop γ\gamma.

The structure group GG and the gauge group 𝒢P\mathcal{G}_{P} operate from the right on PP, resp. on the space of connections 𝒜\mathcal{A}. The holonomy depends by its very construction on a given loop γ\gamma, a connection AA on PP and a base point p∈Pγ⁡(0)p\in P_{\gamma(0)}; hence, it makes sense to consider it as a function on the cartesian product of the space of connections 𝒜\mathcal{A} on PP, the space of loops with values in the structure group GG and the bundle PP itself; later, we will see that it is more precisely a section of some principal bundle over it.

The next Lemma shows how the holonomy behaves w.r.t. the action of GG, resp. of 𝒢\mathcal{G}, on PP, resp. 𝒜\mathcal{A}.

I assume gg, resp. σ\sigma, to be an element of GG, resp. a gauge transformation; I denote by gσg_{\sigma} the function from PP with values in GG canonically associated to σ\sigma via the formula

σ⁡(p)=p​gσ​(p).\sigma(p)=pg_{\sigma}(p).

(This formula makes sense by the transitivity of the action of GG on any fibre of PP.)

3.2. Parallel transport: definition and main properties

The next object I want to define is the parallel transport w.r.t. a connection AA along a general curve γ\gamma.

Definition 3.5.

Let γ\gamma be a curve in MM, not necessarily closed, and let t∈It\in I and p∈Pp\in P, resp. q∈Pq\in P, be such that

π⁡(p)=γ⁡(0),resp.π⁡(q)=γ⁡(t).\pi(p)=\gamma(0),\quad\text{resp.}\quad\pi\left(q\right)=\gamma(t).

I define the parallel transport from pp to qq along γ\gamma from 00 to tt w.r.t. AA, usually denoted by H⁡(A,γ,t,p,q)\partr\!\left(A;\gamma;t;p,q\right), as the unique element of GG obeying the rule

(3.5) γ~A,p​(t)=q​H⁡(A,γ,t,p,q),\widetilde{\gamma}_{A,p}(t)=q\ \partr\!\left(A;\gamma;t;p,q\right),

where γ~A,p\widetilde{\gamma}_{A,p} is the horizontal lift of γ\gamma.

The parallel transport defined by equation (3.5) satisfies two identities similar in spirit to (3.2) and (3.3).

Lemma 3.6.

Given a connection AA on PP, a curve γ\gamma in MM, p∈Pγ⁡(0)p\in P_{\gamma(0)} and q∈Pγ⁡(t)q\in P_{\gamma(t)}, for some tt in the unit interval, general elements hh and kk of GG and a gauge transformation σ∈𝒢\sigma\in\mathcal{G}, the parallel transport of γ\gamma from pp to qq along γ\gamma from 00 to tt satisfies the two following identities:

(3.6) H⁡(A,γ,t,p​g,q​h)\displaystyle\partr\!\left(A;\gamma;t;pg,qh\right) =h−1​H⁡(A,γ,t,p,q)​g;\displaystyle=h^{-1}\partr\!\left(A;\gamma;t;p,q\right)g;
(3.7) H⁡(Aσ,γ,t,p,q)\displaystyle\partr\!\left(A^{\sigma};\gamma;t;p,q\right) =gσ​(q)−1​H⁡(A,γ,t,p,q)​gσ​(p).\displaystyle=g_{\sigma}\!\left(q\right)^{-1}\partr\!\left(A;\gamma;t;p,q\right)g_{\sigma}(p).

By Definition 3.5, one has

γ~A,p​(t)=q​h​H⁡(A,γ,t,p,q​h)=q​H⁡(A,γ,t,p,q).\widetilde{\gamma}_{A,p}(t)=qh\ \partr\!\left(A;\gamma;t;p,qh\right)=q\ \partr\!\left(A;\gamma;t;p,q\right).

By the freeness of the action of GG on PP, one gets

(3.8) H⁡(A,γ,t,p,q​h)=h−1​H⁡(A,γ,t,p,q),∀h∈G.\partr\!\left(A;\gamma;t;p,qh\right)=h^{-1}\partr\!\left(A;\gamma;t;p,q\right),\quad\forall h\in G.

On the other hand, the identity holds

γ~A,p​g​(t)\displaystyle\widetilde{\gamma}_{A,pg}(t) =q​H⁡(A,γ,t,p​g,q)=\displaystyle=q\ \partr\!\left(A;\gamma;t;pg,q\right)=
=γ~A,p​(t)​g=\displaystyle=\widetilde{\gamma}_{A,p}(t)g=
=q​H⁡(A,γ,t,p,q)​g,\displaystyle=q\ \partr\!\left(A;\gamma;t;p,q\right)g,

where the second identity was shown in the proof of Lemma 3.4. It follows therefore

(3.9) H⁡(A,γ,t,p​g,q)=H⁡(A,γ,t,p,q)​g,∀g∈G.\partr\!\left(A;\gamma;t;pg,q\right)=\partr\!\left(A;\gamma;t;p,q\right)g,\quad\forall g\in G.

Combining (3.8) and (3.9), one gets (3.6).

As for the second identity, I make use again of (3.4): it then holds

γ~A,σ⁡(p)​(t)\displaystyle\widetilde{\gamma}_{A,\sigma(p)}\!(t) =σ⁡(q)​H⁡(A,γ,t,σ⁡(p),σ⁡(q))=\displaystyle=\sigma\!\left(q\right)\partr\!\left(A;\gamma;t;\sigma(p),\sigma\left(q\right)\right)=
=σ​(γ~Aσ,p​(t))=\displaystyle=\sigma\!\left(\widetilde{\gamma}_{A^{\sigma},p}(t)\right)=
=σ⁡(q​H⁡(Aσ,γ,t,p,q))=\displaystyle=\sigma\left(q\partr\!\left(A^{\sigma};\gamma;t;p,q\right)\right)=
=σ⁡(q)​H⁡(A,γ,t,σ⁡(p),σ⁡(q)).\displaystyle=\sigma\left(q\right)\partr\!\left(A;\gamma;t;\sigma(p),\sigma\left(q\right)\right).

The freeness of the action of GG implies then

H⁡(Aσ,γ,t,p,q)\displaystyle\partr\!\left(A^{\sigma};\gamma;t;p,q\right) =H⁡(A,γ,t,σ⁡(p),σ⁡(q))=\displaystyle=\partr\!\left(A;\gamma;t;\sigma(p),\sigma\left(q\right)\right)=

where the last identity is a consequence of (3.6). ∎

After having introduced the parallel transport of a curve γ\gamma from 00 to a point tt w.r.t. AA and having discussed some of its properties, I may also introduce another object, namely the parallel transport of the curve γ\gamma from ss to tt, where s,t∈Is,t\in\mathrm{I} satisfy s<ts<t.

First of all, given a curve γ\gamma from the unit interval I\mathrm{I} to MM, and given s∈Is\in\mathrm{I}, let me define a new curve γs\gamma_{s} from the interval [0,1−s]\left[0,1-s\right] by the assignment

γs​(t):=γ⁡(t+s),∀t∈[0,1−s].\gamma_{s}\!(t)\colon=\gamma(t+s),\quad\forall t\in\left[0,1-s\right].
Definition 3.7.

Let γ\gamma be a curve in MM, defined on the unit interval I\mathrm{I}; let then s<ts<t two points in I\mathrm{I}, and pp and qq two points in PP satisfying

π⁡(p)=γ⁡(s),π⁡(q)=γ⁡(t).\pi(p)=\gamma(s),\quad\pi(q)=\gamma(t).

The parallel transport of γ\gamma from pp to qq w.r.t. the connection AA, which I denote by H⁡(A,γ,s,t,p,q)\partr\!\left(A;\gamma;s,t;p,q\right), is the unique element of GG obeying the rule

(3.10) γs~A,p​(t−s)=q​H⁡(A,γ,s,t,p,q).\widetilde{\gamma_{s}}_{A,p}(t-s)=q\partr\!\left(A;\gamma;s,t;p,q\right).

Recalling Equation (3.5), Equation (3.10) is equivalent to

(3.11) H⁡(A,γ,s,t,p,q)=H⁡(A,γs,t−s,p,q).\partr\!\left(A;\gamma;s,t;p,q\right)=\partr\!\left(A;\gamma_{s};t-s;p,q\right).

Lemma 3.6 together with Equation (3.11) implies the useful

Corollary 3.8.

Given a connection AA on PP, a curve γ\gamma in MM, two points s,t∈Is,t\in\mathrm{I} obeying s<ts<t, p∈Pγ⁡(s)p\in P_{\gamma(s)} and q∈Pγ⁡(t)q\in P_{\gamma(t)}, general elements hh and kk of GG and a gauge transformation σ∈𝒢\sigma\in\mathcal{G}, the parallel transport of γ\gamma from pp to qq along γ\gamma from ss to tt satisfies the following identities:

H⁡(A,γ,s,t,p​g,q​h)\displaystyle\partr\!\left(A;\gamma;s,t;pg,qh\right) =h−1​H⁡(A,γ,s,t,p,q)​g;\displaystyle=h^{-1}\partr\!\left(A;\gamma;s,t;p,q\right)g;
H⁡(Aσ,γ,s,t,p,q)\displaystyle\partr\!\left(A^{\sigma};\gamma;s,t;p,q\right) =gσ​(q)−1​H⁡(A,γ,s,t,p,q)​gσ​(p).\displaystyle=g_{\sigma}\!\left(q\right)^{-1}\partr\!\left(A;\gamma;s,t;p,q\right)g_{\sigma}(p).

4. Isomorphisms of principal bundles and generalized gauge transformations

Let P​→𝜋​MP\overset{\pi}{\to}M, P~​→π~​M\widetilde{P}\overset{\widetilde{\pi}}{\to}M two principal bundles over the same manifold MM and with the same structure group GG; the right action of GG on PP, resp. P~\widetilde{P}, is denoted by R∙\raction_{\bullet}, resp. R~∙\widetilde{\raction}_{\bullet}, or simply by (p,g)↦p​g(p,g)\mapsto pg, resp. (p~,g)↦p~​g(\widetilde{p},g)\mapsto\widetilde{p}g, given the case.

Definition 4.1.

Given two principal bundles PP, P~\widetilde{P} as above, a GG-equivariant map σ\sigma from PP to P~\widetilde{P} is a smooth map from PP to P~\widetilde{P} satisfying the two properties:

(4.1) π~∘σ\displaystyle\widetilde{\pi}\circ\sigma =π,\displaystyle=\pi,
σ∘Rg\displaystyle\sigma\circ\raction_{g} =R~g∘σ,∀g∈G.\displaystyle=\widetilde{\raction}_{g}\circ\sigma,\quad\forall g\in G.

The set of all such maps is denoted by 𝒢P,P~\mathcal{G}_{P,\widetilde{P}}.

Remark 4.2.

The set 𝒢P,P\mathcal{G}_{P,P}, for a given principal bundle PP, is the set of gauge transformations of PP.

Given two principal bundles PP, P~\widetilde{P} over MM as above, it is possible to form out of them a manifold as follows:

Definition 4.3.

Given two principal GG-bundles PP and P~\widetilde{P} over the same base space MM, their fibred product, denoted usually by P⊙P~P\odot\widetilde{P}, is defined as

P⊙P~:={(p,p~)∈P×P~:π⁡(p)=π~​(p~)}.P\odot\widetilde{P}\colon=\left\{\left(p,\widetilde{p}\right)\in P\times\widetilde{P}\colon\pi(p)=\widetilde{\pi}\left(\widetilde{p}\right)\right\}.

There is a natural map π¯\overline{\pi} from the fibred product P⊙P~P\odot\widetilde{P} to MM, which is simply

π¯​(p,p~):=π⁡(p)=π~​(p~),(p,p~)∈P⊙P~.\overline{\pi}\left(p,\widetilde{p}\right)\colon=\pi(p)=\widetilde{\pi}\left(\widetilde{p}\right),\quad\left(p,\widetilde{p}\right)\in P\odot\widetilde{P}.

Additionally, P⊙P~P\odot\widetilde{P} receives a right G×GG\times G-action:

(p,p~,(g,h))↦(p​g,p~​h),∀(p,p~)∈P⊙P~,(g,h)∈G×G.\left(p,\widetilde{p};(g,h)\right)\mapsto\left(pg,\widetilde{p}h\right),\quad\forall\left(p,\widetilde{p}\right)\in P\odot\widetilde{P},(g,h)\in G\times G.

It is clear that the above action is free, as both actions of GG on PP and P~\widetilde{P} are free; moreover, considering the fibre

(P⊙P~)x:=π¯−1​({x}),\left(P\odot\widetilde{P}\right)_{x}\colon=\overline{\pi}^{-1}\left(\left\{x\right\}\right),

it follows immediately that the action of G×GG\times G is transitive on it.

These two facts are not incidental, because of the following

Proposition 4.4.

The fibred product P⊙P~P\odot\widetilde{P} is a principal G×GG\times G-bundle over MM, with projection π¯\overline{\pi}.

Proof.

If UU is an open set of MM, let me denote by φU\varphi_{U}, resp. φ~U\widetilde{\varphi}_{U}, the trivialization of PP over UU, resp. of P~\widetilde{P} over UU. A trivialization φ¯U\overline{\varphi}_{U} of P⊙P~P\odot\widetilde{P} over UU may thus be defined via

φ¯:π¯−1​(U)\displaystyle\overline{\varphi}\colon\overline{\pi}^{-1}\!\left(U\right) ⟶U×(G×G)\displaystyle\longrightarrow U\times\left(G\times G\right)
(p,p~)\displaystyle\left(p,\widetilde{p}\right) ⟼(π⁡(p),(pr2∘φU)​(p),(pr2∘φ~U)​(p~)).\displaystyle\longmapsto\left(\pi(p);\left(\pr_{2}\circ\varphi_{U}\right)(p),\left(\pr_{2}\circ\widetilde{\varphi}_{U}\right)\left(\widetilde{p}\right)\right).\,

where pr2\pr_{2} denotes the projection from U×GU\times G onto GG. These maps are invertible, their inverses being given by

φ¯U−1:U×(G×G)\displaystyle\overline{\varphi}_{U}^{-1}\colon U\times\left(G\times G\right) ⟶π¯−1​(U)\displaystyle\longrightarrow\overline{\pi}^{-1}\!\left(U\right)
(x,g,h)\displaystyle\left(x;g,h\right) ⟼(φU−1​(x,g),φ~U−1​(x,h)).\displaystyle\longmapsto\left(\varphi_{U}^{-1}\left(x,g\right),\widetilde{\varphi}_{U}^{-1}\left(x,h\right)\right).

It is clear from their definition that the maps φ¯U\overline{\varphi}_{U} and their inverses are smooth. Hence, I have obtained a trivialization of the fibred product P⊙P~P\odot\widetilde{P}.

For the sake of completeness, let me write down explicitly the transition maps of the G×GG\times G-principal bundle P⊙P~P\odot\widetilde{P}:

φ¯U,V:U∩V\displaystyle\overline{\varphi}_{U,V}\colon U\cap V ⟶Diff⁡(G×G)\displaystyle\longrightarrow\diff\!(G\times G)
x\displaystyle x ⟼RφU,V​(x)×R~φ~U,V​(x),\displaystyle\longmapsto\raction_{\varphi_{U,V}(x)}\times\widetilde{\raction}_{\widetilde{\varphi}_{U,V}(x)},

where φU,V\varphi_{U,V}, resp. φ~U,V\widetilde{\varphi}_{U,V}, are the transition maps of PP, resp. P~\widetilde{P} w.r.t. the trivializations φU\varphi_{U}, φV\varphi_{V}, resp. φ~U\widetilde{\varphi}_{U}, φ~V\widetilde{\varphi}_{V}, for UU, VV any two open subsets of MM with nontrivial intersection. ∎

Remark 4.5.

Let me notice that the fibred product may be also seen as a principal GG-bundle over PP: in fact, by its very definition,

P⊙P~=π∗​(P~),P\odot\widetilde{P}=\pi^{*}\!(\widetilde{P}),

and the latter manifold inherits clearly a principal GG-bundle structure over PP. (Equivalently, the fibred product may be also viewed as a GG-bundle over P~\widetilde{P}, as P⊙P~=π~∗​(P)P\odot\widetilde{P}=\widetilde{\pi}^{*}\!(P).)

Remark 4.6.

The fibred product of two principal bundles over the same base space and with the same structure group may be seen as an analogue of the Whitney sum of vector bundles for principal bundles.

Furthermore, it is clear that there is a canonical isomorphism

P⊙P~≅P~⊙P,P\odot\widetilde{P}\cong\widetilde{P}\odot P,

for any two principal bundles PP, P~\widetilde{P} over the same base space MM.

Now, there is a left action of G×GG\times G on GG specified by the rule:

c:G×G\displaystyle\conj\colon G\times G ⟶Diff⁡(G)\displaystyle\longrightarrow\diff\!(G)
(g,h)\displaystyle(g,h) ⟼c⁡(g,h)​k:=h​k​g−1.\displaystyle\longmapsto\conj\!\left(g,h\right)k\colon=hkg^{-1}.

It is quite evident that the restriction of c\conj to the diagonal subgroup GG of G×GG\times G gives the usual conjugation of GG on itself; therefore, one can speak of the above action as of the generalized conjugation in GG.

Definition 4.7.

Under the same hypotheses as in Definition 4.3, the set of smooth G×GG\times G-equivariant maps from P⊙P~P\odot\widetilde{P} to GG, denoted by C∞​(P⊙P~,G)G×GC^{\infty}\!\!\left(P\odot\widetilde{P},G\right)^{G\times G}, is the subset of C∞​(P⊙P~,G)C^{\infty}\!\!\left(P\odot\widetilde{P},G\right) of those maps KK satisfying the equivariance w.r.t. the generalized conjugation

(4.2) K⁡(p​g,p~​h)=c⁡(g−1,h−1)​K​(p,p~),∀(p,p~)∈P⊙P~,(g,h)∈G×G.K\!\left(pg,\widetilde{p}h\right)=\conj\!\left(g^{-1},h^{-1}\right)K\!\left(p,\widetilde{p}\right),\quad\forall\left(p,\widetilde{p}\right)\in P\odot\widetilde{P},(g,h)\in G\times G.

To a given principal GG-bundle PP over MM, one can associate the canonical map ϕP\phi_{P} on P⊙PP\odot P with values in GG by the rule

(4.3) q=p​ϕP​(p,q),q=p\phi_{P}\!(p,q),

for any pair (p,q)(p,q) in P⊙PP\odot P. Notice that OPENi)i) the definition makes sense, because pp and qq lie in the same fibre and GG operates transitively on each fibre, and OPENi​i)ii) the element ϕP​(p,q)\phi_{P}\!(p,q) is uniquely defined since the action of GG on PP is free.

The following proposition illustrates the main properties of ϕP\phi_{P}.

Proposition 4.8.

The map ϕP\phi_{P} defined by (4.3) is smooth, and satisfies the two identities

(4.4) ϕP​(p,p)\displaystyle\phi_{P}\!(p,p) =e,∀p∈P;\displaystyle=e,\forall p\in P;
(4.5) ϕP​(p,q)\displaystyle\phi_{P}\!\left(p,q\right) =ϕP​(q,p)−1,∀p,q∈P⊙P;\displaystyle=\phi_{P}\!\left(q,p\right)^{-1},\quad\forall p,q\in P\odot P;
(4.6) ϕP​(p​g,q​h)\displaystyle\phi_{P}\!(pg,qh) =g−1​ϕP​(p,q)​h,∀(p,q)∈P⊙P,∀(g,h)∈G×G.\displaystyle=g^{-1}\phi_{P}\!(p,q)h,\quad\forall(p,q)\in P\odot P,\quad\forall(g,h)\in G\times G.
Proof.

By considering a local trivialization φ¯U\overline{\varphi}_{U} of P⊙PP\odot P over U⊂MU\subset M open, one can find a local expression for the map ϕP\phi_{P}:

(x,g,h)​↝ϕP,U​g−1​h,(x;g,h)\overset{\phi_{P,U}}{\leadsto}g^{-1}h,

whence it follows immediately that ϕP\phi_{P} is a smooth map.

Moreover, by its very definition, ϕP\phi_{P} is uniquely determined by (4.3). Taking therefore the pair (p,p)(p,p) in P⊙PP\odot P, by the freeness of the action of GG on PP, both (4.4) and (4.5) follow immediately.

On the other hand, again by (4.3), one gets

p~​h\displaystyle\widetilde{p}h =p​g​ϕP​(p​g,p~​h)=\displaystyle=pg\phi_{P}\!(pg,\widetilde{p}h)=
=p​ϕP​(p,p~)​h,\displaystyle=p\phi_{P}\!(p,\widetilde{p})h,

whence (4.6) follows again by the freeness of the action of GG on any fibre. ∎

Remark 4.9.

The canonical map ϕP\phi_{P} was called by MacKenzie in [8] the division map of PP; the origin of the name lies obviously in its local description, or, equivalently, in its shape for the trivial bundle. On the other hand, Mœrdijk [9] called the division map ϕP\phi_{P} (although working in the more general context of principal bundles with structure groupoids) a cocycle on PP with values in GG; I will use the former name for ϕP\phi_{P}.

This fact finds its motivation in the following

Lemma 4.11.

Any element σ\sigma of 𝒢P,P~\mathcal{G}_{P,\widetilde{P}} is a bijection.

Proof.

The inverse of any bundle morphism σ∈𝒢P,P~\sigma\in\mathcal{G}_{P,\widetilde{P}} is automatically smooth; this can be checked locally or can be viewed as a consequence of Theorem 4.10.

Remark 4.12.

If one considers the case P=P~P=\widetilde{P}, the proof of Lemma 4.11 implies the well-known fact that a gauge transformation, i.e. a bundle endomorphism of PP, is invertible, whence it follows that the set of gauge transformations is a group w.r.t. composition.

4.1. The groupoid of generalized gauge transformations

I consider now the category 𝖡𝗎𝗇G,M\mathsf{Bun}_{G,M} of (smooth) principal bundles over MM with structure group GG. In order to avoid cumbersome notations, a general object of the category 𝖡𝗎𝗇G,M\mathsf{Bun}_{G,M} is labelled by PiP_{i}, for some index ii; the surjective submersion from PiP_{i} to MM is labelled by πi\pi_{i}, and general elements of PiP_{i} are always labelled by the index ii, e.g. pip_{i}, p~i\widetilde{p}_{i}, qiq_{i}. Theorem 4.10 is a general version of the well-known correspondence between bundle endomorphisms of PP (also called gauge transformations) and (smooth) maps on PP with values in GG, equivariant w.r.t. the conjugation action of GG on itself. Moreover, this correspondence can be proved to be an isomorphism of groups, because the set of GG-equivariant maps from PP to GG w.r.t. conjugation inherits a group structure from the multiplication in GG. Obviously, such a group structure is in principle not anymore available, if one considers, instead of a fixed principal GG-bundle PP over MM and its gauge group, all objects of 𝖡𝗎𝗇G,M\mathsf{Bun}_{G,M} and its set of morphisms, i.e. GG-equivariant, fibre-preserving maps from an object PP to another object P~\widetilde{P}, which must not be a priori identical. Lemma 4.11 implies that any morphism of the category 𝖡𝗎𝗇G,M\mathsf{Bun}_{G,M} in the above sense is invertible; hence, the morphisms of the category 𝖡𝗎𝗇G,M\mathsf{Bun}_{G,M} build a groupoid over the objects of the same category.

Let me deal with the following replacement:

P∈𝖮𝖻⁡(𝖡𝗎𝗇G,M)\displaystyle P\in\mathsf{Ob}(\mathsf{Bun}_{G,M}) ↝(P1,P2)∈𝖮𝖻⁡(𝖡𝗎𝗇G,M2),\displaystyle\leadsto\left(P_{1},P_{2}\right)\in\mathsf{Ob}(\mathsf{Bun}_{G,M}^{2}),
C∞​(P,G)G\displaystyle C^{\infty}\!(P,G)^{G} ↝C∞​(P1⊙P2,G)G×G.\displaystyle\leadsto C^{\infty}\!(P_{1}\odot P_{2},G)^{G\times G}.

(Here, I have denoted by 𝖡𝗎𝗇G,M2\mathsf{Bun}_{G,M}^{2} the product category of 𝖡𝗎𝗇G,M\mathsf{Bun}_{G,M} with itself.) It is clear that one can consider the “diagonal” in 𝖮𝖻⁡(𝖡𝗎𝗇G,M2)\mathsf{Ob}\left(\mathsf{Bun}_{G,M}^{2}\right), consisting of pairs of the form (P,P)\left(P,P\right), for P∈𝖡𝗎𝗇G,MP\in\mathsf{Bun}_{G,M}. The GG-equivariant, fibre-preserving isomorphisms of PP (gauge transformations) correspond, on the one hand, to the group C∞​(P,G)GC^{\infty}\!(P,G)^{G}, on the other hand, by Theorem 4.10, to the set C∞​(P⊙P,G)G×GC^{\infty}\!(P\odot P,G)^{G\times G}.

It can be therefore expected that both sets are in bijection; this is in fact true in virtue of the following

Lemma 4.13.

The set C∞​(P,G)GC^{\infty}\!(P,G)^{G} of GG-equivariant maps on PP with values in GG is canonically bijective to the set C∞​(P⊙P,G)G×GC^{\infty}\!(P\odot P,G)^{G\times G} of G×GG\times G-equivariant maps on the fibred product of PP with itself with values in GG.

Proof.

First of all, define a canonical map from C∞​(P⊙P,G)G×GC^{\infty}\!(P\odot P,G)^{G\times G} to C∞​(P,G)C^{\infty}\!(P,G) via the assignment

K∈C∞​(P⊙P,G)G×G↝C∞​(P,G)∋gK​(p):=K⁡(p,p),K\in C^{\infty}\!(P\odot P,G)^{G\times G}\leadsto C^{\infty}\!(P,G)\ni g_{K}\!(p)\colon=K\!(p,p),

i.e., consider simply the restriction to the diagonal of P⊙PP\odot P of any element of C∞​(P⊙P,G)G×GC^{\infty}\!(P\odot P,G)^{G\times G}. One has to prove that such a map gKg_{K}, which is smooth by construction, belongs to C∞​(P,G)GC^{\infty}\!(P,G)^{G}, i.e. one has to prove its GG-equivariance. This is an immediate consequence of the fact that the generalized conjugation of G×GG\times G restricts to the usual conjugation, when taking its restriction from G×GG\times G to its diagonal subgroup.

Consider on the other hand the map ϕP\phi_{P} in (4.3), and to a general element kk of C∞​(P,G)GC^{\infty}\!(P,G)^{G}, associate the map KK defined via the rule

5. Some general constructions for groupoids

In this Section, I discuss some general facts about groupoids; I briefly discuss the concept of product groupoid, and, in more details, the concept of left and right 𝒢\mathcal{G}-spaces, for a general groupoid 𝒢\mathcal{G}. In particular, I introduce the notion of generalized conjugation for groupoids, since a natural notion of conjugation action for groupoids is in some sense elusive. I discuss later the concept of morphisms of groupoids, and later, of equivariant maps between left (and right) groupoid spaces, where the actions may come from distinct groupoids.

To begin with, a general groupoid 𝒢\mathcal{G}, without any assumption on smooth structures, consists of a six-tuple (𝒢,X𝒢,s𝒢,t𝒢,ι𝒢,j𝒢)\left(\mathcal{G},X_{\mathcal{G}},s_{\mathcal{G}},t_{\mathcal{G}},\iota_{\mathcal{G}},j_{\mathcal{G}}\right), whose elements are respectively two sets 𝒢\mathcal{G} (the set of arrows) and X𝒢X_{\mathcal{G}} (the set of points or the set of arrows), two surjective maps s𝒢s_{\mathcal{G}} and t𝒢t_{\mathcal{G}} from 𝒢\mathcal{G} to XX, the source and target of the groupoid, a map ι𝒢\iota_{\mathcal{G}} from XX to 𝒢\mathcal{G}, the identity, and a map j𝒢j_{\mathcal{G}} from 𝒢\mathcal{G} to itself, the inversion of 𝒢\mathcal{G}; these maps satisfy a series of axioms, for which see e.g. [10]. Moreover, there is a well-defined partial product on the set of arrows, which is defined as follows: the set 𝒢2⊂𝒢×𝒢\mathcal{G}_{2}\subset\mathcal{G}\times\mathcal{G} consists of all pairs of elements (g1,g2)\left(g_{1},g_{2}\right) of arrows, such that

s𝒢​(g1)=t𝒢​(g2);s_{\mathcal{G}}(g_{1})=t_{\mathcal{G}}(g_{2});

then, there is an operation from 𝒢2\mathcal{G}_{2} to 𝒢\mathcal{G}, which is denoted as follows

𝒢2\displaystyle\mathcal{G}_{2} →𝒢\displaystyle\to\mathcal{G}
(g1,g2)\displaystyle(g_{1},g_{2}) ↦g1​g2.\displaystyle\mapsto g_{1}g_{2}.

The product has to be associative, whenever it makes sense:

(g1​g2)​g3=g1​(g2​g3),s𝒢​(g1)=t𝒢​(g2),s𝒢​(g2)=t𝒢​(g3).(g_{1}g_{2})g_{3}=g_{1}(g_{2}g_{3}),\quad s_{\mathcal{G}}(g_{1})=t_{\mathcal{G}}(g_{2}),\quad s_{\mathcal{G}}(g_{2})=t_{\mathcal{G}}(g_{3}).

The identity ι𝒢\iota_{\mathcal{G}} and the inversion j𝒢j_{\mathcal{G}} have to satisfy additional identities involving the product, for which I refer to [10].

5.1. The product groupoid of two groupoids 𝒢\mathcal{G}, ℋ\mathcal{H}

Let me introduce briefly the concept of product groupoid of two groupoids 𝒢\mathcal{G} and ℋ\mathcal{H}, which plays a central rôle in the definition of the generalized conjugation for a groupoid 𝒢\mathcal{G} (see Subsection 5.5). Given two groupoids 𝒢\mathcal{G} and ℋ\mathcal{H}, with respective sources, targets, identities and inversions, one may form the product groupoid of 𝒢\mathcal{G} and ℋ\mathcal{H} by putting

  • i)

    the product set 𝒢×ℋ\mathcal{G}\times\mathcal{H} as the set of arrows of the product groupoid;

  • ii)

    the product set X𝒢×XℋX_{\mathcal{G}}\times X_{\mathcal{H}} as the set of objects of the product groupoid;

  • iii)

    the map

    s𝒢×ℋ​(g,h):=(s𝒢​(g),sℋ​(h)),∀(g,h)∈𝒢×ℋ,s_{\mathcal{G}\times\mathcal{H}}\!\left(g,h\right)\colon=\left(s_{\mathcal{G}}(g),s_{\mathcal{H}}(h)\right),\quad\forall(g,h)\in\mathcal{G}\times\mathcal{H},

    as the source map of the product groupoid;

  • iv)

    the map

    t𝒢×ℋ​(g,h):=(t𝒢​(g),tℋ​(h)),∀(g,h)∈𝒢×ℋ,t_{\mathcal{G}\times\mathcal{H}}\!\left(g,h\right)\colon=\left(t_{\mathcal{G}}(g),t_{\mathcal{H}}(h)\right),\quad\forall(g,h)\in\mathcal{G}\times\mathcal{H},

    as the target map of the product groupoid;

  • v)

    the map

    ι𝒢×ℋ​(x,y):=(ι𝒢​(x),ιℋ​(y)),∀(x,y)∈X𝒢×Xℋ,\iota_{\mathcal{G}\times\mathcal{H}}\!(x,y)\colon=\left(\iota_{\mathcal{G}}(x),\iota_{\mathcal{H}}(y)\right),\quad\forall(x,y)\in X_{\mathcal{G}}\times X_{\mathcal{H}},

    as the identity of the product groupoid;

  • vi)

    the map

    j𝒢×ℋ​(g,h):=(j𝒢​(g),jℋ​(h)),∀(g,h)∈𝒢×ℋ,j_{\mathcal{G}\times\mathcal{H}}\!(g,h)\colon=\left(j_{\mathcal{G}}(g),j_{\mathcal{H}}(h)\right),\quad\forall(g,h)\in\mathcal{G}\times\mathcal{H},

    as the inversion of the product groupoid;

  • vii)

    the partial product of the product groupoid is defined by the assignment

    (g1,h1)​(g2,h2):=(g1​g2,h1​h2),s𝒢×ℋ​(g1,h1)=t𝒢×ℋ​(g2,h2).(g_{1},h_{1})(g_{2},h_{2})\colon=(g_{1}g_{2},h_{1}h_{2}),\quad s_{\mathcal{G}\times\mathcal{H}}\!\left(g_{1},h_{1}\right)=t_{\mathcal{G}\times\mathcal{H}}\!\left(g_{2},h_{2}\right).

Notice that the definition of product makes sense by the very definition of the source and target map in the product groupoid. It is immediate to check that all axioms of groupoid are satisfied.

5.2. Morphisms of groupoids

Given two groupoids 𝒢\mathcal{G} and ℋ\mathcal{H}, I want to clarify the notion of morphisms of groupoids.

Definition 5.1.

A morphism from the groupoid 𝒢\mathcal{G} to the groupoid ℋ\mathcal{H} is a pair of maps (Φ,φ)\left(\Phi,\varphi\right), such that the map Φ:𝒢→ℋ\Phi:\mathcal{G}\to\mathcal{H} is a map between the respective sets of arrows and the map φ:X𝒢→Xℋ\varphi:X_{\mathcal{G}}\to X_{\mathcal{H}} is a map between the respective sets of objects.

Moreover, the following two conditions must hold:

  • i)

    the three diagrams must commute

    (5.1) 𝒢→Φℋs𝒢↓↓sℋX𝒢→φXℋ,𝒢→Φℋt𝒢↓↓tℋXℋ→φXℋandX𝒢→φXℋι𝒢↓↓ιℋℋ→Φℋ;\begin{CD}\mathcal{G}@>{\Phi}>{}>\mathcal{H}\\ @V{s_{\mathcal{G}}}V{}V@V{}V{s_{\mathcal{H}}}V\\ X_{\mathcal{G}}@>{\varphi}>{}>X_{\mathcal{H}}\end{CD}\quad,\quad\begin{CD}\mathcal{G}@>{\Phi}>{}>\mathcal{H}\\ @V{t_{\mathcal{G}}}V{}V@V{}V{t_{\mathcal{H}}}V\\ X_{\mathcal{H}}@>{\varphi}>{}>X_{\mathcal{H}}\end{CD}\quad\text{and}\quad\begin{CD}X_{\mathcal{G}}@>{\varphi}>{}>X_{\mathcal{H}}\\ @V{\iota_{\mathcal{G}}}V{}V@V{}V{\iota_{\mathcal{H}}}V\\ \mathcal{H}@>{\Phi}>{}>\mathcal{H}\end{CD}\quad;
  • ii)

    the identity holds

    (5.2) Φ⁡(g1​g2)=Φ⁡(g1)​Φ​(g2),s𝒢​(g1)=t𝒢​(g2).\Phi(g_{1}g_{2})=\Phi(g_{1})\Phi(g_{2}),\quad s_{\mathcal{G}}(g_{1})=t_{\mathcal{G}}(g_{2}).
Remark 5.2.

Notice that the commutativity of the first two diagrams in (5.1) implies that both sides of (5.2) are well-defined.

Moreover, it is immediate to check the identity

Φ∘j𝒢=jℋ∘Φ.\Phi\circ j_{\mathcal{G}}=j_{\mathcal{H}}\circ\Phi.

5.3. The opposite groupoid

I discuss now the notion of opposite groupoid of a groupoid 𝒢\mathcal{G}, which is denoted by 𝒢o​p\mathcal{G}^{\op}.

Set

  • i)

    the set of arrows 𝒢\mathcal{G} of the initial groupoid as the set of arrows of the opposite groupoid;

  • ii)

    the set of objects X𝒢X_{\mathcal{G}} of the initial groupoid as the set of objects of the opposite groupoid;

  • iii)

    the map

    s𝒢o​p:=t𝒢s_{\mathcal{G}}^{\op}\colon=t_{\mathcal{G}}

    as the source map of the opposite groupoid;

  • iv)

    the map

    t𝒢o​p:=s𝒢t_{\mathcal{G}}^{\op}\colon=s_{\mathcal{G}}

    as the target map of the opposite groupoid;

  • v)

    the map

    ι𝒢o​p:=ι𝒢\iota_{\mathcal{G}}^{\op}\colon=\iota_{\mathcal{G}}

    as the identity of the opposite groupoid;

  • vi)

    the map

    j𝒢o​p:=j𝒢j_{\mathcal{G}}^{\op}\colon=j_{\mathcal{G}}

    as the inversion of the opposite groupoid;

  • vii)

    the product ⋅o​p\cdot_{\op}, defined via

    g1⋅o​pg2:=g2​g1,s𝒢o​p​(g1)=t𝒢o​p​(g2),g_{1}\cdot_{\op}g_{2}\colon=g_{2}g_{1},\quad s_{\mathcal{G}}^{\op}(g_{1})=t_{\mathcal{G}}^{\op}(g_{2}),

    as the product on the opposite groupoid.

It is easy to check that the opposite groupoid, as defined above, satisfies all groupoid axioms; moreover, the pair (j𝒢,idX𝒢)\left(j_{\mathcal{G}},\id_{X_{\mathcal{G}}}\right) is an isomorphisms of groupoids from 𝒢\mathcal{G} to the opposite groupoid 𝒢o​p\mathcal{G}^{\op}.

5.4. Left- and right 𝒢\mathcal{G} actions for the groupoid 𝒢\mathcal{G}

Given a groupoid 𝒢\mathcal{G} and a set MM, the next task is to define a natural notion of left 𝒢\mathcal{G}-action on the set MM.

Definition 5.3.

A left 𝒢\mathcal{G}-action of the groupoid 𝒢\mathcal{G} on the set MM consists of a 33-tuple (M,JM,ΨM)\left(M,J_{M},\Psi_{M}\right), where OPENi)i) JMJ_{M} is a map from MM to the set of objects X𝒢X_{\mathcal{G}} of 𝒢\mathcal{G} (which is called the momentum map or shortly the momentum of the action) and OPENi​i)ii) a map ΨM\Psi_{M} from 𝒢×JMM\mathcal{G}\times_{J_{M}}M to MM, where

𝒢×JMM:={(g,m)∈𝒢×M:s𝒢​(g)=JM​(m)}.\mathcal{G}\times_{J_{M}}M\colon=\left\{(g,m)\in\mathcal{G}\times M\colon s_{\mathcal{G}}(g)=J_{M}(m)\right\}.

It is customary to write

ΨM​(g,m):=g​m\Psi_{M}\!\left(g,m\right)\colon=gm

Moreover, the following requirements must hold

  • i)
    JM​(g​m)=t𝒢​(g),∀(g,m)∈𝒢×JMM;J_{M}\!\left(gm\right)=t_{\mathcal{G}}(g),\quad\forall(g,m)\in\mathcal{G}\times_{J_{M}}M;
  • ii)
    g1​(g2​m)=(g1​g2)​m,∀(g1,g2)∈𝒢2,(g1​g2,m)∈𝒢×JMM;g_{1}\left(g_{2}m\right)=\left(g_{1}g_{2}\right)m,\quad\forall(g_{1},g_{2})\in\mathcal{G}_{2},(g_{1}g_{2},m)\in\mathcal{G}\times_{J_{M}}M;

    observe that Condition OPENi)\mathnormal{i}) implies that the previous identity is well-defined.

  • iii)
    ι𝒢​(JM​(m))​m=m,∀m∈M.\iota_{\mathcal{G}}\left(J_{M}(m)\right)m=m,\quad\forall m\in M.
Remark 5.4.

The definition of right 𝒢\mathcal{G}-action is similar, the only difference being that one has to switch the rôles of the source and target maps; consequently, the map ΨM\Psi_{M} goes from the product M×JM𝒢M\times_{J_{M}}\mathcal{G} to MM, and is denoted by

ΨM​(m,g):=m​g.\Psi_{M}(m,g)\colon=mg.

Equivalently, a right 𝒢\mathcal{G}-action is a left 𝒢o​p\mathcal{G}^{\op}-action, and the switch between the two actions is simply given by the inversion j𝒢j_{\mathcal{G}}.

5.5. The generalized conjugation of 𝒢\mathcal{G}

It is well-known that there is in general no natural notion of conjugation action on a groupoid. Nonetheless, as it is discussed in [11], the conjugation action on an abstract group GG may be viewed as a specialization of the so-called generalized conjugation discussed at the beginning of Section 4; the latter action admits an easy generalization to the context of groupoids, which I am now going to discuss in detail.

First of all, consider the product groupoid 𝒢2\mathcal{G}^{2} of 𝒢\mathcal{G} with itself; the aim is to construct a right action of 𝒢2\mathcal{G}^{2} on 𝒢\mathcal{G}. The first ingredient one needs is a map from 𝒢\mathcal{G} to the product of the set of objects X𝒢X_{\mathcal{G}} with itself, the momentum of the (right) generalized conjugation: namely, I define

Jc​(g):=(s𝒢​(g),t𝒢​(g)),∀g∈𝒢.J_{\conj}\!\left(g\right)\colon=\left(s_{\mathcal{G}}(g),t_{\mathcal{G}}(g)\right),\quad\forall g\in\mathcal{G}.

Consequently, the set 𝒢×Jc𝒢2\mathcal{G}\times_{J_{\conj}}\mathcal{G}^{2} has the form

𝒢×Jc𝒢2={(g3,g1,g2)∈𝒢3:{t𝒢​(g1)=s𝒢​(g3)t𝒢​(g2)=t𝒢​(g3)}.\mathcal{G}\times_{J_{\conj}}\mathcal{G}^{2}=\left\{\left(g_{3};g_{1},g_{2}\right)\in\mathcal{G}^{3}\colon\begin{cases}t_{\mathcal{G}}(g_{1})&=s_{\mathcal{G}}(g_{3})\\ t_{\mathcal{G}}(g_{2})&=t_{\mathcal{G}}(g_{3})\end{cases}\right\}.

It makes thus sense to define the map Ψc\Psi_{\conj} from 𝒢×Jc𝒢2\mathcal{G}\times_{J_{\conj}}\mathcal{G}^{2} to 𝒢\mathcal{G} by the rule

(5.3) Ψc​(g3,g1,g2):=g2−1​g3​g1,\Psi_{\conj}\!\left(g_{3};g_{1},g_{2}\right)\colon=g_{2}^{-1}g_{3}g_{1},

where, for the sake of simplicity, g2−1:=j𝒢​(g2)g_{2}^{-1}\colon=j_{\mathcal{G}}(g_{2}).

These data fit into a right 𝒢2\mathcal{G}^{2}-action on 𝒢\mathcal{G} in the sense of Definition 5.3, as shown in the following

Proposition 5.5.

The triple (𝒢2,Jc,Ψc)\left(\mathcal{G}^{2},J_{\conj},\Psi_{\conj}\right) defines a right 𝒢2\mathcal{G}^{2}-action on 𝒢\mathcal{G}, which is called the generalized conjugation of 𝒢\mathcal{G}.

Proof.

First of all, let me compute, for any triple (g3,g1,g2)\left(g_{3};g_{1},g_{2}\right) in 𝒢×Jc𝒢2\mathcal{G}\times_{J_{\conj}}\mathcal{G}^{2}, the following expression:

(Jc∘Ψc)​(g3,g1,g2)\displaystyle\left(J_{\conj}\circ\Psi_{\conj}\right)\!\left(g_{3};g_{1},g_{2}\right) =Jc​(g2−1​g3​g1)=\displaystyle=J_{\conj}\!\left(g_{2}^{-1}g_{3}g_{1}\right)=
=by definition of Jc​(s𝒢​(g2−1​g3​g1),t𝒢​(g2−1​g3​g1))=\displaystyle\overset{\text{by definition of $J_{\conj}$}}{=}\left(s_{\mathcal{G}}\!\left(g_{2}^{-1}g_{3}g_{1}\right),t_{\mathcal{G}}\!\left(g_{2}^{-1}g_{3}g_{1}\right)\right)=
=(s𝒢​(g1),t𝒢​(g2−1))=\displaystyle=\left(s_{\mathcal{G}}(g_{1}),t_{\mathcal{G}}(g_{2}^{-1})\right)=
=(s𝒢​(g1),s𝒢​(g2))=\displaystyle=\left(s_{\mathcal{G}}(g_{1}),s_{\mathcal{G}}(g_{2})\right)=
=s𝒢2​(g1,g2),\displaystyle=s_{\mathcal{G}^{2}}\!\left(g_{1},g_{2}\right),

which proves the first requirement for (𝒢2,Jc,Ψc)\left(\mathcal{G}^{2},J_{\conj},\Psi_{\conj}\right) to be a right 𝒢2\mathcal{G}^{2} action.

Second, I compute explicitly

Ψc​(Ψc​(g3,g1,g2),h1,h2)\displaystyle\Psi_{\conj}\!\left(\Psi_{\conj}\!\left(g_{3};g_{1},g_{2}\right);h_{1},h_{2}\right) =Ψc​(g2−1​g3​g1,h1,h2)=\displaystyle=\Psi_{\conj}\!\left(g_{2}^{-1}g_{3}g_{1};h_{1},h_{2}\right)=
=h2−1​(g2−1​g3​g1)​h1=\displaystyle=h_{2}^{-1}\left(g_{2}^{-1}g_{3}g_{1}\right)h_{1}=
=(g2​h2)−1​g3​(g1​h1)=\displaystyle=\left(g_{2}h_{2}\right)^{-1}g_{3}(g_{1}h_{1})=
=Ψc​(g3,g1​h1,g2​h2),\displaystyle=\Psi_{\conj}\!\left(g_{3};g_{1}h_{1},g_{2}h_{2}\right),

whenever the identity makes sense.

Finally, one has to compute

Ψc(g;ι𝒢2(Jc(g)))\displaystyle\Psi_{\conj}\!\left(g_{;}\iota_{\mathcal{G}^{2}}\!\left(J_{\conj}(g)\right)\right) =Ψc​(g,ι𝒢​(s𝒢​(g)),ι𝒢​(t𝒢​(g)))=\displaystyle=\Psi_{\conj}\!\left(g;\iota_{\mathcal{G}}(s_{\mathcal{G}}(g)),\iota_{\mathcal{G}}(t_{\mathcal{G}}(g))\right)=
=ι𝒢​(t𝒢​(g))−1​g​ι𝒢​(s𝒢​(g))=\displaystyle=\iota_{\mathcal{G}}(t_{\mathcal{G}}(g))^{-1}g\iota_{\mathcal{G}}(s_{\mathcal{G}}(g))=
=g,∀g∈𝒢,\displaystyle=g,\quad\forall g\in\mathcal{G},

whence the claim follows. ∎

Remark 5.6.

There is another right 𝒢2\mathcal{G}^{2}-action on 𝒢\mathcal{G}; in fact, one can consider the map J¯c\overline{J}_{\conj} from 𝒢\mathcal{G} to X𝒢×X𝒢X_{\mathcal{G}}\times X_{\mathcal{G}} given by

J¯c​(g):=(t𝒢​(g),s𝒢​(g)),\overline{J}_{\conj}(g)\colon=\left(t_{\mathcal{G}}(g),s_{\mathcal{G}}(g)\right),

and the map Ψ¯c\overline{\Psi}_{\conj} from 𝒢×J¯c𝒢2\mathcal{G}\times_{\overline{J}_{\conj}}\mathcal{G}^{2} to 𝒢\mathcal{G} via

Ψ¯c​(g3,g1,g2):=g1−1​g3​g2.\overline{\Psi}_{\conj}\!\left(g_{3};g_{1},g_{2}\right)\colon=g_{1}^{-1}g_{3}g_{2}.

The action of Proposition 5.5, as well as the action of Remark 5.6, are called both generalized conjugations of 𝒢\mathcal{G}, because they are the natural analogues of the generalized conjugation of a group GG, which I have briefly discussed at the beginning of Section 4.

Notice that there are also two left generalized conjugations of 𝒢\mathcal{G}: namely, take

{JcL​(g):=Jc(g),ΨcL(g1,g2;g3):=g2g3g1−1,J¯cL​(g):=J¯c(g),Ψ¯cL(g1,g2;g3):=g1g3g2−1,\begin{cases}J_{\conj}^{L}(g)&\colon=J_{\conj}(g),\quad\Psi_{\conj}^{L}\!\left(g_{1},g_{2};g_{3}\right)\colon=g_{2}g_{3}g_{1}^{-1},\\ \overline{J}_{\conj}^{L}(g)&\colon=\overline{J}_{\conj}(g),\quad\overline{\Psi}_{\conj}^{L}\!\left(g_{1},g_{2};g_{3}\right)\colon=g_{1}g_{3}g_{2}^{-1},\end{cases}

for (g1,g2,g3)\left(g_{1},g_{2};g_{3}\right) in 𝒢2×JcL𝒢\mathcal{G}^{2}\times_{J_{\conj}^{L}}\mathcal{G}, resp. 𝒢2×J¯cL𝒢\mathcal{G}^{2}\times_{\overline{J}_{\conj}^{L}}\mathcal{G}. The proof that both triples (𝒢,JcL,ΨcL)\left(\mathcal{G},J_{\conj}^{L},\Psi_{\conj}^{L}\right) and (𝒢,J¯cL,Ψ¯cL)\left(\mathcal{G},\overline{J}_{\conj}^{L},\overline{\Psi}_{\conj}^{L}\right) define both left 𝒢2\mathcal{G}^{2}-actions is immediate.

5.6. Equivariant maps between groupoid-spaces

I want to define and discuss the concept of equivariant map between groupoid-spaces; here, by groupoid-space, I mean a set MM acted on (from the left or from the right) by a groupoid 𝒢\mathcal{G}.

For our purposes, let me consider the following general situation: given a left 𝒢\mathcal{G}-space (M,JM,ΨM)\left(M,J_{M},\Psi_{M}\right) and a left ℋ\mathcal{H}-space (N,JN,ΨN)\left(N,J_{N},\Psi_{N}\right) respectively, where 𝒢\mathcal{G}, ℋ\mathcal{H} are any two groupoids and MM, NN any two sets.

Definition 5.7.

A (twisted) equivariant map between the left 𝒢\mathcal{G}-space MM and the left ℋ\mathcal{H}-space NN is a triple (Θ,Φ,φ)\left(\Theta,\Phi,\varphi\right), where Θ\Theta is a map from the set MM to the set NN, and the pair (Φ,φ)\left(\Phi,\varphi\right) is a morphism from the groupoid 𝒢\mathcal{G} to the groupoid ℋ\mathcal{H} in the sense of Definition 5.1.

Moreover, one imposes the commutativity of the following diagrams:

  • i)
    M→ΘNJM↓↓JNX𝒢→φXℋ;\begin{CD}M@>{\Theta}>{}>N\\ @V{J_{M}}V{}V@V{}V{J_{N}}V\\ X_{\mathcal{G}}@>{\varphi}>{}>X_{\mathcal{H}}\end{CD}\quad;
  • ii)
    𝒢×JMM→Φ×Θℋ×JNNΨM↓↓ΨNM→ΘN\begin{CD}\mathcal{G}\times_{J_{M}}M@>{\Phi\times\Theta}>{}>\mathcal{H}\times_{J_{N}}N\\ @V{\Psi_{M}}V{}V@V{}V{\Psi_{N}}V\\ M@>{\Theta}>{}>N\end{CD}
Remark 5.8.

The first commutative diagram in Definition 5.7 implies that Φ×Θ\Phi\times\Theta maps 𝒢×JMM\mathcal{G}\times_{J_{M}}M to ℋ×JNN\mathcal{H}\times_{J_{N}}N, as the following explicit computation shows:

JN​(Θ​(m))\displaystyle J_{N}\left(\Theta(m)\right) =φ​(JM​(m))=\displaystyle=\varphi(J_{M}(m))=
=φ​(s𝒢​(g))=\displaystyle=\varphi(s_{\mathcal{G}}(g))=
=sℋ​(Φ⁡(g)),∀(g,m)∈𝒢×JMM.\displaystyle=s_{\mathcal{H}}(\Phi(g)),\quad\forall(g,m)\in\mathcal{G}\times_{J_{M}}M.

Usually, the second diagram is encoded in the following identity:

Θ⁡(g​m)=Φ⁡(g)​Θ​(m),∀(g,m)∈𝒢×JMM,\Theta(gm)=\Phi(g)\Theta(m),\quad\forall(g,m)\in\mathcal{G}\times_{J_{M}}M,

which corresponds clearly to the usual definition of (twisted by Φ\Phi) equivariance of a map Θ\Theta from a left GG-space to a left HH-space, for GG, HH usual groups.

6. Applications to bundles on the space of loops or paths

In the present section, I interpret the holonomy as a gauge transformation of a bundle over the space of loops in the manifold MM, and similarly the parallel transport as a generalized gauge transformation on bundles over the space of loops or, more generally, paths in MM.

Consider first the space of free loops in MM, which is denoted by L​M\mathrm{L}M; by the word “free”, one means loops in MM without a specified base point. There are canonical, smooth maps from the product manifold L​M×I\mathrm{L}M\times\mathrm{I} to MM, the evaluation map and the evaluation map at 00, defined respectively via

(6.1) ev⁡(γ,t):\displaystyle\ev\left(\gamma;t\right)\colon =γ⁡(t);\displaystyle=\gamma(t);
(6.2) ev0⁡(γ,t):\displaystyle\ev_{0}\left(\gamma;t\right)\colon =γ⁡(0).\displaystyle=\gamma(0).

Using the maps (6.1) and (6.2), one can construct two principal GG-bundles on the cylinder L​M×I\mathrm{L}M\times\mathrm{I} as follows: consider a fixed principal GG-bundle PP over MM, and take the pull-backs

ev∗⁡P\displaystyle\ev^{*}P ={(γ,t,p)∈L​M×I×P:π⁡(p)=γ⁡(t)};\displaystyle=\left\{\left(\gamma;t;p\right)\in\mathrm{L}M\times\mathrm{I}\times P\colon\pi(p)=\gamma(t)\right\};
ev0∗​P\displaystyle\ev_{0}^{*}P ={(γ,t,p)∈L​M×I×P:π⁡(p)=γ⁡(0)}.\displaystyle=\left\{\left(\gamma;t;p\right)\in\mathrm{L}M\times\mathrm{I}\times P\colon\pi(p)=\gamma(0)\right\}.

The canonical projections from both bundles onto L​M×I\mathrm{L}M\times\mathrm{I} map any 33-tuple to the first two arguments; this allows us to write the fibred product of ev∗⁡P\ev^{*}P and ev0∗​P\ev_{0}^{*}P as

ev0∗P⊙ev∗P={(γ;t;p,p~)∈LM×I×P×P:π(p)=γ(0),π(p~)=γ(t)}.\ev_{0}^{*}P\odot\ev^{*}P=\left\{\left(\gamma;t;p,\widetilde{p}\right)\in\mathrm{L}M\times\mathrm{I}\times P\times P\colon\pi(p)=\gamma(0),\quad\pi\left(\widetilde{p}\right)=\gamma(t)\right\}.

Choosing a background connection AA on PP, one can define (see Section 3) the holonomy w.r.t. AA and the parallel transport w.r.t. AA. The holonomy is an element of GG, depending on a loop γ\gamma and on a chosen base point p∈Pp\in P, satisfying π⁡(p)=γ⁡(0)=ev0⁡(γ,t)\pi(p)=\gamma(0)=\ev_{0}(\gamma,t). Hence, it may be viewed as a map on the pulled-back bundle ev0∗​P\ev_{0}^{*}P with values in GG, which depends additionally on the choice of a connection AA on PP. Moreover, Equation (3.2) of Lemma 3.4 implies that the holonomy is a GG-equivariant map from ev0∗​P\ev_{0}^{*}P to GG; thus, it may be viewed as a gauge transformation of ev0∗​P\ev_{0}^{*}P. Similarly, the parallel transport w.r.t. a chosen connection AA depends on a curve γ\gamma in MM, some t∈It\in\mathrm{I}, and two points in PP, (p,q)(p,q), satisfying π⁡(p)=γ⁡(0)\pi(p)=\gamma(0) and π⁡(q)=γ⁡(t)\pi(q)=\gamma(t); hence, the parallel transport may be viewed as a function on the fibred product of ev0∗​P\ev_{0}^{*}P and ev∗⁡P\ev^{*}P with values in GG. Moreover, Equation (3.6) of Lemma 3.6 guarantees that the parallel transport is G×GG\times G-equivariant w.r.t. the generalized conjugation introduced at the beginning of Section 4. Thus, parallel transport defines a generalized gauge transformation between the bundle ev0∗​P\ev_{0}^{*}P and ev∗⁡P\ev^{*}P, depending on the choice of a connection AA.

From now on, the holonomy H(A)|∙∙\partr(A)\arrowvert_{\bullet}^{\bullet}, viewed as a gauge transformation of ev0∗​P\ev_{0}^{*}P, is denoted simply by H(A)|01\partr(A)\arrowvert_{0}^{1}, whereas the parallel transport H⁡(A,∙,∙,∙,∙)\partr\!\left(A;\bullet;\bullet;\bullet,\bullet\right) as a generalized gauge transformation is denoted by H(A)|0∙\partr(A)\arrowvert_{0}^{\bullet}. Theorem 4.10 of Section 4 implies that the parallel transport H(A)|0∙\partr(A)\arrowvert_{0}^{\bullet} induces a bundle (iso)morphism from ev0∗​P\ev_{0}^{*}P to ev∗⁡P\ev^{*}P, which is denoted by ΦA\Phi_{A} in order to make explicit its dependence on the chosen connection AA.

I now want to inspect now more carefully the dependence on the chosen connection AA of the isomorphism ΦA\Phi_{A}, in view of the computations done in Subsection 5.7 of Section 5. First, write down the isomorphism ΦA\Phi_{A} explicitly:

ΦA​(γ,t,p)=(γ,t,q​H⁡(A,γ,t,p,q)),\Phi_{A}\!\left(\gamma;t;p\right)=\left(\gamma;t;q\partr\!\left(A;\gamma;t;p,q\right)\right),

where π⁡(p)=γ⁡(0)\pi(p)=\gamma(0), and q∈Pq\in P is any point satisfying π⁡(q)=γ⁡(t)\pi\left(q\right)=\gamma(t).

It is well-known that the gauge group 𝒢\mathcal{G} operates on the space of connections 𝒜\mathcal{A} by pull-back. Considering now a gauge transformation σ\sigma and taking the pull-back of the connection AA w.r.t. σ\sigma, the morphism ΦA\Phi_{A} changes as follows:

(6.3) Φσ∗​A​(γ,t,p)\displaystyle\Phi_{\sigma^{*}A}\left(\gamma;t;p\right) =(γ,t,p~​H⁡(σ∗​A,γ,t,p,p~))=\displaystyle=(\gamma;t;\widetilde{p}\ \partr\!\left(\sigma^{*}A;\gamma;t;p,\widetilde{p}\right))=
=(γ,t,p~​gσ​(p~)−1​H⁡(A,γ,t,p,p~)​gσ​(p))=\displaystyle=(\gamma;t;\widetilde{p}\ g_{\sigma}\!\left(\widetilde{p}\right)^{-1}\!\partr\!\left(A;\gamma;t;p,\widetilde{p}\right)\!g_{\sigma}(p))=
=(γ,t,σ−1​(p~)​H⁡(A,γ,t,p​gσ​(p),p~))=\displaystyle=\left(\gamma;t;\sigma^{-1}\!\left(\widetilde{p}\right)\ \partr\!\left(A;\gamma;t;p\ g_{\sigma}(p),\widetilde{p}\right)\right)=
=(γ,t,σ−1​(p~​H⁡(A,γ,t,σ⁡(p),p~)))=\displaystyle=\left(\gamma;t;\sigma^{-1}\!\left(\widetilde{p}\ \partr\!\left(A;\gamma;t;\sigma(p),\widetilde{p}\right)\right)\right)=
=σ−1​(ΦA​(γ,t,σ⁡(p))).\displaystyle=\sigma^{-1}\left(\Phi_{A}\left(\gamma;t;\sigma(p)\right)\right).

The main argument used in the proof of the above equation is Identity (3.7) of Lemma 3.6; this identity admits an interpretation in terms of equivariant maps between groupoid-spaces, as introduced in Subsection 5.6 of Section 5.

I need some technical arguments to make the statement more precise. Assume ff to be a smooth map from some manifold LL to MM; then

Lemma 6.1.

Every gauge transformation of PP induces a gauge transformation of the pulled-back bundle f∗​Pf^{*}P.

Proof.

Consider a general gauge transformation σ∈𝒢P\sigma\in\mathcal{G}_{P}. By definition,

f∗​P={(l,p)∈L×P:f⁡(l)=π⁡(p)};f^{*}P=\left\{\left(l,p\right)\in L\times P\colon f(l)=\pi(p)\right\};

consider then a general point (l,p)(l,p) in f∗​Pf^{*}P. Define a morphism σf\sigma_{f} from f∗​Pf^{*}P to itself as follows:

σf​(l,p):=(l,σ⁡(p)).\sigma_{f}\!\left(l,p\right)\colon=\left(l,\sigma(p)\right).

One has then to show that σf\sigma_{f} is well-defined, that it respects the fibres of f∗​Pf^{*}P and that it is GG-equivariant; bijectivity, and hence invertibility, follows from Lemma 4.11 of Section 4.

Since π∘σ=π\pi\circ\sigma=\pi, it follows that the image of a point in f∗​Pf^{*}P still belongs to f∗​Pf^{*}P. By its very definition, σf\sigma_{f} is fibre-preserving. The GG-equivariance of σf\sigma_{f} is immediate.

Notice that the map taking σ\sigma to σf\sigma_{f} is clearly a homomorphism of groups from 𝒢P\mathcal{G}_{P} to 𝒢f∗​P\mathcal{G}_{f^{*}P}. ∎

The gauge group of PP, 𝒢P\mathcal{G}_{P}, can be viewed as a groupoid, where the set of objects X𝒢PX_{\mathcal{G}_{P}} is simply a point, namely, one can consider this point as PP, an object of the category 𝖡𝗎𝗇G,M\mathsf{Bun}_{G,M}; source map and target map are simply

s𝒢P​(σ)=t𝒢P​(σ)=P;s_{\mathcal{G}_{P}}(\sigma)=t_{\mathcal{G}_{P}}(\sigma)=P;

identity is simply

ιP​(P)=idP.\iota_{P}(P)=\id_{P}.

Finally, the inversion is clearly

j𝒢P​(σ)=σ−1.j_{\mathcal{G}_{P}}(\sigma)=\sigma^{-1}.

Moreover, as already seen at the end of Section 2, the gauge group 𝒢P\mathcal{G}_{P} operates on the space of connections on PP, 𝒜P\mathcal{A}_{P}; it is easy to see that 𝒜P\mathcal{A}_{P} is a right 𝒢P\mathcal{G}_{P}-space in the sense explained in Subsection 5.4 of Section 5.

I want to construct a morphism of groupoids between 𝒢P\mathcal{G}_{P} and the product groupoid of the groupoid of generalized gauge transformations of the space of loops (or paths) in MM with itself. The groupoid of generalized gauge transformations, for a manifold MM and group GG, is denoted by 𝒢G,M\mathcal{G}_{G,M} (hence, it follows 𝒢G,M,P1,P2=C∞!​(P1⊙P2,G)G×G\mathcal{G}_{G,M,P_{1},P_{2}}=C^{\infty}!\left(P_{1}\odot P_{2},G\right)^{G\times G}, P1P_{1} and P2P_{2} being two principal GG-bundles over MM).

Lemma 6.2.

The pair (ΦP,φP)\left(\Phi_{P},\varphi_{P}\right), where

{φP​(P):=(ev0∗​P,ev∗⁡P)ΦP​(σ):=(σev0,σev),\begin{cases}\varphi_{P}(P)&\colon=\left(\ev_{0}^{*}P,\ev^{*}P\right)\\ \Phi_{P}(\sigma)&\colon=\left(\sigma_{\ev_{0}},\sigma_{\ev}\right)\end{cases},

is a morphism in the sense of Definition 5.1 from the groupoid 𝒢G,L​M2\mathcal{G}_{G,\mathrm{L}M}^{2}, for any manifold MM and any Lie group GG..

Proof.

According to Definition 5.1, one has to show first the commutativity of the three diagrams of (5.1); this is immediate, because of the definition of source map, target map and identity for the product groupoid of the groupoid of generalized gauge transformations of L​M\mathrm{L}M (see Subsection 5.1 for more details).

Property (5.2) follows immediately from Lemma 6.1 and from the definition of product of a product groupoid. ∎

Using now all arguments sketched in Section 4 and 5, one can restate Identity (3.7) of Lemma 3.6 as follows:

Proposition 6.3.

The triple (H(∙)|0∙,ΦP,φP)\left(\partr(\bullet)\arrowvert_{0}^{\bullet},\Phi_{P},\varphi_{P}\right) defines an equivariant map from the space of connections 𝒜P\mathcal{A}_{P}, viewed as a right 𝒢P\mathcal{G}_{P}-space, to the groupoid 𝒢G,L​M\mathcal{G}_{G,\mathrm{L}M}, resp. 𝒢G,P​M\mathcal{G}_{G,\mathrm{P}\!M} of generalized gauge transformations of the space of loops (resp. paths) in MM, viewed as a right 𝒢G,L​M2\mathcal{G}_{G,\mathrm{L}M}^{2}-, resp. 𝒢G,P​M2\mathcal{G}_{G,\mathrm{P}\!M}^{2}-,space via the generalized conjugation introduced in Subsection 5.5. (By H(∙)|0∙\partr(\bullet)\arrowvert_{0}^{\bullet}, I mean the map associating to a connection AA the corresponding parallel transport as a generalized gauge transformation.)

Proof.

First of all, the momentum J𝒜PJ_{\mathcal{A}_{P}} is simply given by

J𝒜P​(A):=P,∀A∈𝒜P.J_{\mathcal{A}_{P}}\!(A)\colon=P,\quad\forall A\in\mathcal{A}_{P}.

With this definition in mind, and recalling the arguments of Subsection 5.5, one gets immediately the commutativity of the first diagram in Definition 5.7.

It remains to show the commutativity of the second diagram. This is an immediate consequence of the explicit computation done in Subsection 5.7 together with Identity (3.7) of Lemma 3.6. ∎

An immediate consequence of Proposition 6.3, together with Identity (3.3) of Lemma 3.4, is given by

Corollary 6.4.

The holonomy map H(∙)|01\partr(\bullet)\arrowvert_{0}^{1}, assigning to any connection AA in 𝒜P\mathcal{A}_{P} the gauge transformation of the bundle ev0∗​P\ev_{0}^{*}P defined by the holonomy w.r.t. AA, is an equivariant map from the space of connections on PP to the gauge group of ev0∗​P\ev_{0}^{*}P w.r.t. the conjugation.

6.0.1. A consequence of Corollary 6.4: the Wilson loop map

In this subsubsection, I discuss an important consequence of Corollary 6.4, namely the construction of the so-called Wilson loop map; this map plays an important rôle in the framework of Topological Quantum Field Theories, in particular Chern–Simons Theory.

To begin with, notice that the holonomy map H(A)|01\partr(A)\arrowvert_{0}^{1}, for any given connection AA, defines immediately a section of the associated bundle Ad⁡(ev0∗​P)\Ad\!(\ev_{0}^{*}P) on L​M×I\mathrm{L}M\times\mathrm{I} w.r.t. conjugation. For our purposes, it is better to view the holonomy map H(A)|01\partr(A)\arrowvert_{0}^{1} as a map from the pulled-back bundle ev⁡(0)∗​P\ev(0)^{*}P over L​M\mathrm{L}M, where ev⁡(0)\ev(0) is defined via

ev⁡(0)​(γ):=γ​(0)\ev(0)(\gamma)\colon=\gamma(0)

(see also the beginning of Subsection 6.1). Similarly, this holonomy map, denoted again by H(A)|01\partr(A)\arrowvert_{0}^{1}, descends to a section of the associated bundle Ad⁡(ev⁡(0)∗​P)\Ad\!(\ev(0)^{*}P); this bundle is associated to ev⁡(0)∗​P\ev(0)^{*}P via the conjugation of GG. More generally, dropping out the explicit dependence on connections, the holonomy map H(∙)|01\partr(\bullet)\arrowvert_{0}^{1} may be viewed as a map from the cartesian product of 𝒜P\mathcal{A}_{P}, the space of connections on PP, with the principal bundle ev⁡(0)∗​P\ev(0)^{*}P on the space of loops L​M\mathrm{L}M, to the group GG; this map satisfies, by Corollary 6.4, two kinds of equivariance, namely w.r.t. the GG-action on ev⁡(0)∗​P\ev(0)^{*}P and w.r.t. the 𝒢P\mathcal{G}_{P}-action on 𝒜P\mathcal{A}_{P}. Consider now a representation (V,ρ)(V,\rho) of GG, namely a (real or complex) vector space VV endowed with a group homomorphism ρ\rho from GG to the automorphism group of VV. Composing the holonomy map with ρ\rho, one gets a map from the product 𝒜P×ev⁡(0)∗​P\mathcal{A}_{P}\times\ev(0)^{*}P to the linear group G​L​(V)GL(V); the aforementioned equivariance properties hold again, since ρ\rho is a group homomorphism. Finally, one can take the trace in the endomorphism ring of VV of the composite map ρ∘H(∙)|01\rho\circ\partr(\bullet)\arrowvert_{0}^{1}; the result of these operations is denoted by

Wρ​(A,γ,p):=TrV⁡(ρ⁡(H⁡(A,γ,p))),W_{\rho}(A;\gamma;p)\colon=\tr_{V}\!\left(\rho(\partr\!\left(A;\gamma;p\right))\right),

which is called Wilson loop map WρW_{\rho} w.r.t. the representation ρ\rho. It is clearly a (real or complex, depending on the representation VV) function on 𝒜P×ev⁡(0)∗​P\mathcal{A}_{P}\times\ev(0)^{*}P.

The cyclicity of the trace TrV\tr_{V}, together with Corollary 6.4, implies the two following invariance properties of the Wilson loop map:

(6.4) Wρ​(A,γ,p​g)\displaystyle W_{\rho}(A;\gamma;pg) =Wρ​(A,γ,p),∀g∈G,\displaystyle=W_{\rho}(A;\gamma;p),\quad\forall g\in G,
(6.5) Wρ​(Aσ,γ,p)\displaystyle W_{\rho}(A^{\sigma};\gamma;p) =Wρ​(A,γ,p),∀σ∈𝒢.\displaystyle=W_{\rho}(A;\gamma;p),\quad\forall\sigma\in\mathcal{G}.

Let me spend a few words on the space of connections on PP, 𝒜P\mathcal{A}_{P}: as already seen at the end of Section 2, the gauge group 𝒢P\mathcal{G}_{P} operates on the right on 𝒜P\mathcal{A}_{P}. It would naturally be interesting to analyse the properties of the gauge group action of 𝒢P\mathcal{G}_{P} on 𝒜P\mathcal{A}_{P} and to find suitable conditions for this action to be free; in fact, there could be in principle gauge transformations fixing connections, e.g. if the structure group GG possesses a nontrivial centre, there are constant gauge transformations fixing any given connection. Therefore, in order to consider the moduli space of connections on PP, i.e. the quotient space 𝒜P/𝒢P\mathcal{A}_{P}/\mathcal{G}_{P}, one has to consider only the space 𝒜P∗\mathcal{A}_{P}^{*} of irreducible connections, which is the subset of 𝒜P\mathcal{A}_{P} on which the group 𝒢P∗\mathcal{G}_{P}^{*} (the quotient group of 𝒢P\mathcal{G}_{P} by the centre of the structure group GG, which may be viewed as a normal subgroup of 𝒢P\mathcal{G}_{P}). Hence, it makes sense to consider the quotient space 𝒜P∗/𝒢P∗\mathcal{A}_{P}^{*}/\mathcal{G}_{P}^{*}, which one can view as the base space of a principal 𝒢P∗\mathcal{G}_{P}^{*}-bundle, whose total space is 𝒜P∗\mathcal{A}_{P}^{*}; it is not my plan to discuss the local structure of this quotient space, thus I do not enter into the details of the construction of suitable topologies on it.

Equations (6.4) and (6.5) imply immediately the following

Proposition 6.5.

For any linear representation (V,ρ)(V,\rho) of GG, the structure group of PP, the Wilson loop map

𝒜P∗×ev⁡(0)∗​P∋(A,γ,p)↦Wρ​(A,γ,p)\mathcal{A}_{P}^{*}\times\ev(0)^{*}P\ni(A;\gamma;p)\mapsto W_{\rho}(A;\gamma;p)

descends to a function WρW_{\rho} on the product of the moduli space of connections 𝒜P∗/𝒢P∗\mathcal{A}_{P}^{*}/\mathcal{G}_{P}^{*} with the space of loops L​M\mathrm{L}M.

7. Some consequences of flatness related to holonomy and parallel transport

Motivated by Proposition 6.3 of Section 6, which allows us to parameterize particular generalized gauge transformations of the space of loops or paths in MM by connections on a given background bundle PP over MM in an equivariant way, I am interested now in the restriction of the equivariant map of Proposition 6.3 to the space of flat connections, on which the gauge group of PP also operates. Before entering into the details, I need some technical facts about connections on the fibred product (see Section 4 for more details) of any two principal bundles.

7.1. Connections on the fibred product of two principal bundles

Assume PP, P~\widetilde{P} to be objects (a priori distinct) of the category 𝖡𝗎𝗇G,M\mathsf{Bun}_{G,M}, endowed with respective connections AA and A~\widetilde{A}. A general tangent vector to the fibred product P⊙P~P\odot\widetilde{P} at a point (p,p~)\left(p,\widetilde{p}\right) can be written as a pair (Xp,Xp~)\left(X_{p},X_{\widetilde{p}}\right), where XpX_{p}, resp. Xp~X_{\widetilde{p}}, is a tangent vector to PP at pp, resp. to P~\widetilde{P} at p~\widetilde{p}. By the very definition of the projection π¯\overline{\pi} from P⊙P~P\odot\widetilde{P} onto MM, the tangent vector (Xp,Xp~)\left(X_{p},X_{\widetilde{p}}\right) is vertical if and only if

T(p,p~)⁡π¯​(Xp,Xp~)=Tp⁡π⁡(Xp)=Tp~⁡π~​(Xp~)=0,\tange\!_{\left(p,\widetilde{p}\right)}{\overline{\pi}}\left(X_{p},X_{\widetilde{p}}\right)=\tange\!_{p}{\pi}\left(X_{p}\right)=\tange\!_{\widetilde{p}}{\widetilde{\pi}}\left(X_{\widetilde{p}}\right)=0,

i.e.  if and only if both components of (Xp,Xp~)\left(X_{p},X_{\widetilde{p}}\right) are vertical.

As seen in Section 2, the connection AA, resp. A~\widetilde{A}, specifies a smooth splitting of the tangent bundle of PP, resp. P~\widetilde{P}, into vertical and AA-horizontal bundle, resp. A~\widetilde{A}-horizontal bundle. Hence, one can write any tangent vector XpX_{p}, resp. Xp~X_{\widetilde{p}}, to PP at pp, resp. to P~\widetilde{P} at p~\widetilde{p}, as

Xp=Xpv+Xph,resp.Xp~=Xp~v+Xp~h.X_{p}=X_{p}^{v}+X_{p}^{h},\quad\text{resp.}\quad X_{\widetilde{p}}=X_{\widetilde{p}}^{v}+X_{\widetilde{p}}^{h}.

Thus, any tangent vector (Xp,Xp~)\left(X_{p},X_{\widetilde{p}}\right) to P⊙P~P\odot\widetilde{P} at (p,p~)\left(p,\widetilde{p}\right) has a unique splitting

(7.1) (Xp,Xp~)=(Xpv,Xp~v)+(Xph,Xp~h).\left(X_{p},X_{\widetilde{p}}\right)=\left(X_{p}^{v},X_{\widetilde{p}}^{v}\right)+\left(X_{p}^{h},X_{\widetilde{p}}^{h}\right).

It is clear from the definition of the action of G×GG\times G on P⊙P~P\odot\widetilde{P} that the sets of all vectors of the form (Xph,Xp~h)\left(X_{p}^{h},X_{\widetilde{p}}^{h}\right) in (7.1), for any pair (p,p~)∈P⊙P~(p,\widetilde{p})\in P\odot\widetilde{P}, specify a G×GG\times G-invariant family of subspaces. Therefore, by the arguments recalled in Section 2, to the splitting (7.1) belongs obviously the connection 11-form

(A⊙A~)(p,p~)​(Xp,Xp~):=(Ap​(Xp),A~p~​(Xp~)),\left(A\odot\widetilde{A}\right)_{\!\left(p,\widetilde{p}\right)}\!\left(X_{p},X_{\widetilde{p}}\right)\colon=\left(A_{p}\!\left(X_{p}\right),\widetilde{A}_{\widetilde{p}}\!\left(X_{\widetilde{p}}\right)\right),

which is called the fibred product connection of the connections AA and A~\widetilde{A}; the fibred product connection A⊙A~A\odot\widetilde{A} is a 𝔤⊕𝔤\mathfrak{g}\oplus\mathfrak{g}-valued form on P⊙P~P\odot\widetilde{P}. Notice that the fibred product connection A⊙A~A\odot\widetilde{A} can be written alternatively as the restriction of the connection on the product P×P~P\times\widetilde{P} given by

(prP∗​A,prP~∗​A~),\left(\pr_{P}^{*}\!A,\pr_{\widetilde{P}}^{*}\!\widetilde{A}\right),

where prP\pr_{P}, resp. prP~\pr_{\widetilde{P}}, denotes the projection of P⊙P~P\odot\widetilde{P} onto PP, resp. P~\widetilde{P}, to P⊙P~P\odot\widetilde{P}.

Recall that a connection AA on PP is flat, if it satisfies the equation

(7.2) d​A+12​[A,A]=0.\mathrm{d}A+\frac{1}{2}{\left[{\,{A}\,,\,{A}\,}\right]}=0.

An equivalent characterisation of flatness of a connection AA, viewed as a way of splitting the tangent bundle of PP into vertical and AA-horizontal bundle, is that the AA-horizontal bundle specifies an integrable distribution over PP, i.e. the Lie bracket of any two AA-horizontal vectors is again horizontal. From the latter characterisation of the fibred product connection A⊙A~A\odot\widetilde{A}, it follows that the fibred product connection is flat if and only if both AA and A~\widetilde{A} are flat; it is a consequence of Equation (7.2).

Given now a bundle morphism σ\sigma from PP to P~\widetilde{P} in the sense of Definition 4.1, one can construct a map σ⊙σ−1\sigma\odot\sigma^{-1} from P⊙P~P\odot\widetilde{P} to P~⊙P\widetilde{P}\odot P as follows:

(σ⊙σ−1)​(p,p~):=(σ⁡(p),σ−1​(p~)),∀(p,p~)∈P⊙P~.\left(\sigma\odot\sigma^{-1}\right)\left(p,\widetilde{p}\right)\colon=\left(\sigma(p),\sigma^{-1}\left(\widetilde{p}\right)\right),\quad\forall\ \left(p,\widetilde{p}\right)\in P\odot\widetilde{P}.
Lemma 7.1.

The fibred product map σ⊙σ−1\sigma\odot\sigma^{-1}, for any bundle morphism σ\sigma from PP to P~\widetilde{P}, is a bundle morphism from the fibred product P⊙P~P\odot\widetilde{P} to P~⊙P\widetilde{P}\odot P (notice that both are G×GG\times G-bundles).

There is a fibred product connection A~⊙A\widetilde{A}\odot A on P~⊙P\widetilde{P}\odot P. The pull-back of a fibred product connection A~⊙A\widetilde{A}\odot A on P~⊙P\widetilde{P}\odot P w.r.t. the fibred product map σ⊙σ−1\sigma\odot\sigma^{-1} equals a fibred product connection B⊙B~B\odot\widetilde{B} on P⊙P~P\odot\widetilde{P}, if and only if

7.2. Composition properties and inversion of the parallel transport

In this subsection, I state and prove two technical lemmata, which will be used later, when proving the two theorems on the consequences of flatness of the reference connection AA on both holonomy and parallel transport, viewed respectively as a gauge transformation of the pulled-back bundle ev0∗​P\ev_{0}^{*}P on L​M×I\mathrm{L}M\times\mathrm{I} (or also ev⁡(0)∗​P\ev(0)^{*}P on L​M\mathrm{L}M) and as a generalized gauge transformation on L​M\mathrm{L}M or, more generally P​M\mathrm{P}\!M.

In fact, I will prove later how the parallel transport behaves w.r.t. the composition and inversion of paths.
